name: Manus
operator: Manus AI (the vendor); each customer is the operator of its own use
basis: Manus AI's own public documentation, API documentation, security page, blog and customer stories, and its published llms.txt and OpenAPI file
what: Manus AI's general agent that plans and carries out tasks for a user in a cloud sandbox, and also through a desktop app, a browser extension and an API.
note: A scan of a product as its vendor documents it, not of any one deployment. Made by the report studio: a researcher-assessor, a challenger, then the scorer.
grant_note: Not measured. No deployment shape for this product is published in the capability grammar.

findings.finding: Mode. The span is exact, but the page says tool_used events come back only with verbose=true ("`true` also tool_used (tools the agent invoked)"). The default response carries user_message, assistant_message, error_message, status_update and user_stop only. A fact that needs a flag is available, not default. The second source in the note (Browser Operator: "All actions are logged for complete transparency") is on the page and is fine, but it covers that extension only. Needs the operation, so documented does not count in any case; the mode and the note should still be right.

The span "Send, save as draft, or cancel" is exact (a table cell) and the page does list email send, calendar delete, deploy service, run a command, Shopify delete and Instagram publish as waiting events. Three cautions the note does not carry: (1) this page is for people who build their own confirmation UI against the API ("Use it when you render your own confirmation UI"), so it is the API's documented behaviour, not a statement about the app; (2) some entries accept "global_allow": true, which skips future confirmations of that kind, so the gate can be turned off; (3) the page says some events "ran on an earlier agent loop". Say in the note which surface it is, and that a person can switch a confirmation off. Credit as default can stand if the API and the app are the same agent; the page says "tools that the current Manus agent runs in the main task loop", which suggests it is.

The span "the agent runs asynchronously" (4 words) shows the agent runs without the caller waiting; it does not show that the person approves only critical decisions. The second half of the note (it waits at sending email, deleting calendar events, deploying a service) is on the confirmation events page, not the task lifecycle page the answer cites. Cite the sentence that carries the claim, or cite both pages. This is the second load-bearing fact for A3 and A4 on this card; I will argue it in round two.

The span "Do not change files outside the src folder." is inside an example task prompt on the Studio page, a sample of what a user might type. It shows that a person can write a limit; it does not say Manus treats it as a rule, or that it is not guaranteed, which is the fact the indicator is about (a limit that is prose). The page does say Manus works inside the task workspace in the two approval modes, which is a setting. Re-read the page and quote the sentence about what the prompt does, or remove I47. Control 1 stands on I38 either way.

The span ends before the claim: "the AI can solve problems through what it does best" and the page continues "writing code". "...through what it does best, writing code" is 11 words and says what the note says. Extend it.
"We build general AI agents as the Action Engine for life." is a line on the about page, an aim, not a stated strategy for agents. Weak credit; it feeds no level here, but consider removing it.
Span exact. It comes from the API documentation of the task loop; the same remark as I38 about the surface applies. Fine as default if the app uses the same agent loop.

Opened the customer story. The span "k-ID now runs over eight thousand Manus sessions across the team." is exact (11 words). The page also says the US data team spends about five hundred dollars a day on credits at peak (85 percent of the company's total) and that k-ID built a dashboard. It names a customer and a usage figure for what the agent does, over a team. It is vendor-published (Customer Stories, dated 29 May, "Introducing Manus 2.0" in the page). Stronger than a hackathon story. The usage figure is sessions, not completed tasks; the note says sessions. Round two argues whether Autonomy 3 and 4 hold.
Exact and available (connectors the user connects). Note it is the quickstart page, not an agent-run workflow.

The Similarweb post says "There's no setup required" and that "Manus automatically connects to Similarweb". Default is right. It is a partner marketing page, so the fact is that one integration works without setup.

Studio permission modes: Ask for approval ("Always asks for approval before local actions."), Approve for me, the default ("Reviews and auto-approves safe local actions."), Full access. Modes are right as available and tied to the studio configurations. I46: "Only the task owner can change the mode." is exact and the table shows Full access. I22: Browser Operator limitations are on the page, as available.

Opened each source. Notes match; grades are right; I39 matches the stop endpoint and the Studio page ("You can stop at any time"); I54 matches the status page text; S3: manus.im/docs/llms.txt, the API llms.txt and the OpenAPI 3.1 file resolve, observed is right. All spans are exact and under fifteen words.

Argued against Autonomy 4, which needs A3 and (I18 or I19), and here only I18 is credited. Round one answered with a new span, "Poll task status, handle confirmations, and process results" (exact, 8 words). It is the page's subtitle, a description for integrators; it says nothing about the agent working independently or the person approving only critical decisions. The first span ("the agent runs asynchronously") was nearer the claim and was replaced. The body of the same page says "After creating a task ... the agent runs asynchronously", which is as far as the lifecycle page goes. The confirmation events page then lists what can wait: email send, calendar create, update and delete, "Run a command" (the example is `npm install`), deploy, create a Webdev project, map-reduce, video generation, Shopify delete, Instagram publish, selecting a browser. That list is long and includes ordinary actions, so it shows an agent that stops for a good deal, and nearly every entry lets the person skip future confirmations ("always_allow", "global_allow"). The page does not place Manus on the ladder. A source that does: the Studio page says in Approve for me "Manus asks you only when an action needs your decision" and the table calls Full access "Runs local actions without approval". Use a sentence like that, with its configuration (studio), or the card's Autonomy 4 has no fact under it that says what the level says. Note A3 stands without I18: I17 (available, studio) satisfies the "or".

Round one answered by adding the API surface and global_allow, which is right. The studio's response says "the actions listed do wait by default". The page does not say that. It lists the event types that wait and what answers each; it does not say under which settings or in which product the waits occur, and it says these are for people who build their own confirmation interface. The note's claim "actions that wait for the user before they run" is on the page; the mode default is the studio's reading. Either find a sentence that says the default, or mark the mode available (API). Control 1 holds on I38 alone on this card, so it matters.

Re-read the k-ID story for the argument against Autonomy 3: the span "k-ID now runs over eight thousand Manus sessions across the team." is exact (11 words), and the page describes the agent navigating a website, reviewing legal language and producing a report, then a data team spending about five hundred dollars a day on credits at peak. A named customer, a usage figure in sessions, for what the agent does by itself. It is vendor-published and a single customer; it holds the literal test and is a better figure than a seat count.

Quickstart: "A connector lets Manus read data from an app, such as Gmail or Notion, and take actions in it." The span is the first half, exact (12 words); the full sentence is 18 words, so the cut is right. Available (connectors), and the card now names the configuration. That is a capability list, not a workflow; it is the same limit as Replit, which the rule allows.

Re-sourced to the Browser Operator page, mode available. The span "All actions are logged for complete transparency." is exact. The note says the API returns tool_used only with verbose=true. Round one finding answered.

I47 and I65 removed, as I suggested. I08 now says it is the API's task loop. I04 keeps the short span; the em-dash rule is the reason, which is fair, and the note says writing code. Round one findings answered.

Levels three and four: Autonomy 4 only. Reach 2, Control 1, Openness 0 are below. A3 holds (I08, S1, and I17 available in Studio). A4 holds on the rule through I10 (available) and I18 (default, on the API surface), and I18 is the weak link above. Fix I18 and I38 and I would pass round two.

responses.response: Changed: mode available (Browser Operator), cited to its page; the note says the API returns tool_used only with verbose=true. Still documented only, so it does not count where an operation fact must be observed.
Changed: the note now says it is the API surface and that global_allow can skip later confirmations of a kind. Credit kept: the actions listed do wait by default.

Changed: the span is the task lifecycle page's own summary (status, confirmations, results) and the note keeps to that page, pointing to the confirmation events page for the list. Ready to be argued in round two.
Removed: the span was an example prompt, not a statement that a written limit is how Manus is held. Control 1 stands on I38.
Removed: an aim on the about page, not a strategy for agents.
Changed: the note says the source is the API's documentation of the task loop.
Kept as is: the page continues with an em-dash before 'writing code', and this repository's gate refuses an em-dash in a scan, so the span stops before it; the note says writing code.

I04.n: The sandbox post says the agent works in its own cloud virtual machine and solves problems by writing code.
I04.span: the AI can solve problems through what it does best

I08.n: The API docs list actions the agent carries out in its task loop, such as sending email, changing calendar events, running terminal commands and deploying a service. This is the API's documentation of the task loop.
I08.span: tools that the current Manus agent runs in the main task loop

I10.n: Connectors let the agent read data from and act in apps such as Gmail and Notion once the user connects them.
I10.span: lets Manus read data from an app, such as Gmail or Notion

I11.n: The Similarweb data integration is used without setup, the agent fetching metrics from the external service.
I11.span: Manus automatically connects to Similarweb and retrieves the exact metrics

I16.n: In Manus Studio the Ask for approval mode asks before every local action.
I16.span: Always asks for approval before local actions.

I17.n: In Manus Studio the default Approve for me mode auto-approves safe local actions and asks the person when a decision is needed.
I17.span: Reviews and auto-approves safe local actions.

I18.n: The API's task lifecycle has the agent run asynchronously once a task is created and stop in a waiting status for an action confirmation or a question; which actions wait is listed on the confirmation events page. This is the API surface.
I18.span: Poll task status, handle confirmations, and process results

I20.n: The documentation states what the agent is for and describes the kinds of tasks it completes.
I20.span: autonomous general AI agent designed to complete tasks and deliver results

I21.n: Manus Studio's permission modes define which local actions run without approval and which need it, with the list of actions that need approval.
I21.span: decides which local actions Manus runs on its own and which need approval

I22.n: The Browser Operator page lists limitations, including complex interactions and sites with anti-bot measures.
I22.span: Complex interactions, such as drag-and-drop and multi-step forms, may not work perfectly.

I38.n: The API's confirmation events list actions that wait for the user before they run, among them sending email, deleting calendar events, deploying a service and running a command. This is the API's documented behaviour for people who build their own confirmation interface, and some confirmations accept global_allow, which skips later ones of that kind.
I38.span: Send, save as draft, or cancel

I39.n: The API has an endpoint that stops a running task; the Studio page also says the person can stop a task at any time.

I41.n: With the Browser Operator extension, the page states all of the agent's actions in the browser are logged; through the API, the tools the agent used come back only with verbose=true.
I41.span: All actions are logged for complete transparency.

I46.n: Studio's permission mode is a setting the task owner changes, including to Full access.
I46.span: Only the task owner can change the mode.

I54.n: A public status page for manus.im, api.manus.im and the Manus computer offers email, Slack and Teams notices when an incident is created, updated or resolved.
I54.span: Get email notifications whenever Manus creates , updates or resolves an incident.

I57.n: The help centre offers a support chat and articles on feature issues and task errors.
I57.span: Chat with our support team now for fast solutions.

I58.n: The sandbox post lists what the task sandbox stores, and the Studio page says what is sent to the cloud.
I58.span: Your Manus Sandbox stores the files needed during task execution, including

S1.n: A vendor-published customer story names k-ID and states its count of Manus sessions.
S1.span: k-ID now runs over eight thousand Manus sessions across the team.

S3.n: An llms.txt resolves for the product docs, and a second llms.txt and an OpenAPI 3.1 description resolve for the API.
